nameStory: The common bladderwort gets its name from the tiny bladder-like traps hidden along its underwater stems. These microscopic 'bladders' work like vacuum pumps, sucking in water fleas and other tiny creatures in less than a millisecond - making this innocent-looking aquatic plant one of nature's most efficient underwater predators!
description: Common bladderwort is a floating carnivorous plant that lives entirely in the water, never rooted to the bottom. Its feathery, thread-like underwater stems drift freely through ponds and lakes, while bright yellow snapdragon-like flowers peek above the surface on tall stalks. The whole plant creates dense, tangled mats that can stretch several feet across, looking almost like submerged green hair flowing in the current.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers shaped like tiny snapdragons, about half an inch tall, rising 4-8 inches above the water surface on leafless stalks. Each flower has a distinctive pouched lower lip and feels papery to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Feathery, thread-like underwater stems that feel soft and slimy when pulled from the water. No true leaves - instead, the green branching segments look like fine green hair or delicate underwater ferns.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Free-floating with no roots anchoring to the bottom. Forms dense, tangled mats just below the water surface that feel springy when you run your hand through them.

idTips.label: Bladders
idTips.description: Tiny clear or yellowish bubble-like traps scattered along the underwater stems, about the size of a pinhead. You'll need to look closely - they feel like small bumps when you run the stems between your fingers.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, green underwater stems that branch repeatedly in all directions, creating a complex web. They break easily and release tiny air bubbles when crushed, with a faint grassy smell.

habitat: Quiet ponds, lakes, slow-moving streams, and beaver ponds throughout New England, typically in acidic to neutral water. Prefers shallow areas with some protection from strong currents, often found mixed with other aquatic plants like water lilies and pondweeds. Most common in waters 1-8 feet deep where sunlight can penetrate to support photosynthesis.

seasonality.spring: New growth begins as water warms, with fresh green shoots emerging from overwintering buds. Plants start forming dense underwater mats but flowers haven't appeared yet.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with bright yellow flowers prominently displayed above the water surface from June through August. This is the easiest time to spot and identify the species.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and plants begin forming winter buds called turions. The underwater vegetation starts to die back and turn brownish.
seasonality.winter: Most of the plant dies back, surviving as small, dense winter buds (turions) that sink to the bottom and remain dormant until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Each tiny bladder trap can suck in prey faster than a human can blink - in just 0.5 milliseconds! The plant creates a vacuum inside each bladder, and when tiny water creatures brush against trigger hairs, a trapdoor flies open and the victim gets sucked in like being caught in an underwater tornado.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other submerged aquatic plants like water milfoil or hornwort, but common bladderwort is the only free-floating one with bright yellow snapdragon flowers. Memory trick: 'Yellow snapdragons floating free' - if it's rooted to the bottom or has different colored flowers, it's not common bladderwort.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being carnivorous, bladderworts are completely harmless to humans and fish - their traps only catch microscopic prey like water fleas, mosquito larvae, and tiny worms. Many people don't realize these delicate aquatic plants are actually fierce predators of the microscopic world.
compareHints: Common bladderwort is the largest and most robust of New England's bladderworts, with the biggest flowers and most substantial underwater growth. Purple bladderwort has pink to purple flowers instead of yellow, while lesser bladderwort has much smaller, paler yellow flowers. Horned bladderwort grows in wet soil rather than floating freely in open water.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Horned bladderwort stands out from its many bladderwort relatives by having the most prominent horn-like spur and by growing in terrestrial or semi-aquatic conditions rather than fully underwater.
Small swollen bladderwort is smaller and more delicate than common bladderwort and lacks the large inflated floats of swollen bladderwort.
Among New England's bladderworts, purple bladderwort is unique for its purple flowers – most others have yellow blooms.
Swollen bladderwort is the largest of New England's aquatic bladderworts and the only one with truly prominent inflated stems that feel spongy to the touch.
Intermediate bladderwort differs from common bladderwort by having fewer, slightly smaller flowers and more delicate overall appearance.
Humped bladderwort is much smaller and more delicate than common bladderwort, forming thin surface mats rather than robust underwater colonies.
Northeastern bladderwort is distinguished from other New England bladderworts by its lavender-purple flowers and preference for very shallow water or bog margins.

Hidden-fruit Bladderwort is unique among New England's bladderworts for keeping its flowers at or below the water surface, while most relatives like Common and Purple Bladderwort hold their blooms well above water on conspicuous stalks.
Lesser bladderwort is distinguished from common bladderwort by its much smaller size and more delicate appearance overall.
Among New England's bladderworts, zigzag bladderwort is unique for its terrestrial zigzag growth habit - most other bladderworts either float in water or grow upright from water.
Distinguished from common bladderwort by much finer, more delicate underwater stems and smaller overall size.
